Preface to the Five Lamps’ Strict Lineage:
I have heard that in the transmission of the Dharma of our school, the divergent paths and side-entrances must be strictly guarded against.

Once a deviation occurs, it leads not only to the error of falsely claiming to be a distant successor—like the fallacy of "stealing the jade and pretending it is a chicken"—but gradually results in using slander as a "spiritual pivot" (jīfēng).
To reduce [the Dharma] to mere shouts and blows is to sever the authentic lineage; it is nearly extinct.

One must know that the ancestral law has its source, its culmination, and its branches and streams, as well as its direct heirs. From the Sixth Patriarch at Caoxi, the lineage subsequently divided into two schools:
Nanyue and Qingyuan. These constitute the source. Under Nanyue were Linji, Guiyang, Fayan, and Yunmen, while under Qingyuan was Caodong; these form the five [houses].
As for the main lineages: from Linji came Xinghua and Yangqi; from Yunmen came Zhimen and Xuedou;
and from Caodong came Touzi and Furong. As for the branches: following these were Yuanwu, Huqiu, Tiantong, and Changlu.
Although they possessed distinct portions of the direct lineage, within them the dust of the alms bowl was transmitted from master to disciple—like father to son, and grandson to great-grandson.
Yet, from the profound past down through several dozen generations, the transmission of the lamp has continued like the dynastic histories of a nation or the genealogical records of a clan.
Regarding the lineage of emperors, kings, sages, and saints, who would dare to falsely attribute a single person or a single word to it, thereby defiling the prestige of their family records?

Since time immemorial, when great matters concerning the causes and conditions of world-abiding *kalyāṇamitras* have arisen, they have sometimes awaited the raising of the *kan* (the staff) and the *ti* (the question). But who was it that established the school? Who...

To raise the banner of this school, who has not transmitted the robe and succeeded the whisk? There have been none whose brilliance was not as clear as stars spread across the heavens, such that they could be distinguished upon one's palm or fingers.

Within this lineage, there have occasionally been those capable of not merely following the literal text; their names were recorded in the Tripitaka and their deeds were engraved upon stone by the various mountains.
This is solely because they have attained their respective lineages. Otherwise, branches and leaves would proliferate in confusion, and separate walls would be erected within the palace.
One must surely rely on the sound and attach oneself to the reputation [of the tradition] to be able to hope for the original moment when the flower was held up and the bowl was placed down. Alas!

It is truly as it has been said that the teachings of Shen, Han, Yang, and Mo were a source of dread to Confucius and Mencius. I once read the *Zhengming lu* (Record of Correcting Names) of the Chan school; its discussion of Xuetings Wanzong...

Yunmen’s single case is like a sharp blade cutting through bamboo; one suddenly beholds the mark of the edge. This serves as a sufficient warning for those throughout the world and in future generations who merely inherit empty echoes.

Therefore, he wrote [the *Record*] to examine and verify the lineages of the school, establishing his own doctrine, and composed the "Chapter on Teacher-Disciple Succession" in three parts to clarify the fundamental principles.
His contribution to supporting the Chan gate was such that his merit was no less than that of Yu the Great. If one were to say he attained realization without a teacher...
Wu: This is yet another delusion within delusions. Why must you point toward fox dens and rabbit burrows, engaging in debate before the blind and the mute?

Master Feheshan of Jing Mountain possesses great vision and insight; he has rectified the errors regarding the continuity and rupture of the Five Lamps and compiled the *Yantong* in twenty-five fascicles.
For instance, in his preface to Nanyue, he minutely analyzes the claims concerning Tianhuang, addressing all such erroneous and reckless assertions regarding the offering of incense.

These [criticisms] are all subject to refutation and rejection. Not only do they reveal what scholars have previously failed to uncover, but through them, the *Chuan deng lu* (Transmission of the Lamp) and the genealogical records may both flow like rivers and stand firm like mountains throughout the ten thousand years of past and future. It is my hope that future scholars, upon reading this book, will reflect on its name and contemplate its meaning;
that they will know the source from which their own bodies emerge and the lineage they inherit, thereby clearly demonstrating how one might laugh at the act of "throwing a needle."
It would be appropriate to simply return it to its original site on Vulture Peak as established by Nāgārjuna; what need is there for further elaboration?

Written with utmost reverence and prostrations by Wei Chengxian, Compiler of the Imperial Academy of Academicians and Secretary of the Hanlin Academy, who has been promoted one grade, during the eighth month of autumn in the year of Xinmao, the eighth year of the Shunzhi era.
Preface to the *Wǔdēng Yántǒng* (The Five Lamps Adorning the Lineage).
Since the three teachings have been practiced, the Way of Chan has flourished greatly up to the present day. Yet, the Chan lineage has become increasingly muddled by now.
The Great Chan Master Fěiyǐn felt a profound sense of anxiety regarding this. Last autumn, before he had yet departed for Jìngshān, [he wrote] nine...
When the moon reached its fullness, I traveled from Fuyan to Hezuo and invited him to accompany me to Yunjian, where we stayed at the Xiaokunshan Hermitage.
Together with the lay practitioner Licai, we examined the old editions of the *Five Lamps* (Wudeng Huiyuan), investigating the lineages of transmission and tracing their origins.

We excavated the caverns of doubt from the past and established the authentic records for future generations. This work is luminous and majestic, serving as a revelation for Buddhism since its inception.
This is the primary standard for the circulation of the teachings. Since the time of Jingzhao in the Dongshan school, there have not been no subsequent publications;
however, as these were transmitted like shadows following echoes, they resulted in errors in commentary and glosses that far exceeded the "lu-yu-hai-xi" mistakes common among Confucianists.
I could not help but sigh deeply at this. We three men pledged ourselves to be public-spirited and cautious; tracing the source and analyzing the currents, we collected five volumes.

All of these were painstakingly sought out by Master Bai Chan, who transcribed them by hand into complete volumes. At that time, I was deeply concerned that there would be no one to take charge of the task.
Lacking the means to raise the necessary funds, I personally witnessed the hardships at that time. Moved by deep regret, I took up the burden myself and returned south with my scrolls.

I used my own resources to purchase pearwood blocks and assembled craftsmen to carve the matrices. Subsequently, I arrived at Jinsu Temple and, together with Master Bai, further refined and corrected the text.

I personally oversaw the proofreading, urging them morning and night until the work was completed in early spring; the joy that followed can well be imagined. Including this along with previous editions, the total count is as follows: [insert number].
This work comprises twenty-five fascicles, collectively titled *The Five Lamps’ Strict Lineage*. This past autumn, the Elder of Mount Jing sent me the preface by Shi Cai;
upon reading it, its clarity shone like the sun, sufficient to cause those who peddle counterfeit vessels to seal their lips.
I am neither learned nor a man of letters, yet I cannot remain silent regarding the profound intent behind the title. Why is this?
The West (India) possesses the five lineages of the Dhyāna pulse; the East (China) possesses the five leaves of the Chan school.

Though they branch into five—and even into hundreds, thousands, ten-thousands, millions, and billions—they ultimately converge into a single source. Thus, regarding the orthodox lineage, one must examine how the five heterodoxies return to the One.

Regarding the establishment of banners and the founding of teachings, as they gradually reach the inconceivable, one must verify the intercalary lineages. How much more so when households are separated and gates divided; there can be no doubt that such concerns exist.

When short and long reeds are played upon, they harmonize and then diverge; as they diverge and then harmonize again, their underlying unity must be discerned. Now, investigation (*he*), verification (*ji*), and discernment (*bian*) are all matters of rigor.
Rigor is the opposite of severity, yet neither laxity nor excess should prevail; indeed, it is precisely through severity that one achieves rigor. In my youth, I studied Confucianism;

Preface to the Five Lamps:

Clarifying the Lineage In ancient times, when the Dharma lineage of our Bhagavān was transmitted from master to disciple, there were four groups of seven in the Western Heavens (India) and two groups of three in the Eastern Land (China).

These branched into two streams and further divided into five schools. As these schools and lineages became clearly manifest, the authentic succession of masters provided a firm basis for faith, which dawned with clarity.

At that time, [the records] were so certain as to serve as definitive evidence for posterity; thus, while the lion’s roar resounded throughout the world, there was no report of those who feigned or plagiarized.

Alas, since the Great Dharma has entered its autumnal decline and the hearts of men have ceased to follow antiquity, even the publication of the *Xu lüe* (Continued Abridgment) cannot entirely avoid errors such as confusing the crane with the wild goose.

The corruption of the lineage records (*zōngpǔ*) is extreme; moreover, the circumstantial accounts lack documentation, and surnames and names are forcibly fabricated, throwing everything into disorder.
The succession of a thousand autumns opens the way for the rectification of myriad errors. It is like damming the Yangtze and the Yellow River; where could it possibly come to rest? Alas!
The lineages have become muddled and confused, and the life of wisdom hangs by a thread. All who possess breath and blood harbor grief over the corruption of the refined tradition;
how much more so for Master Bai-chi, who takes the transmission of the Way as his own responsibility—could he not look upon this with deep anxiety and profound concern? If he does not...
I have exerted my strength to rectify this matter, lest future students be led into a realm of gloom and obscurity.
Having no other choice, I have undertaken this project of carving the woodblocks; my investigations are thorough and my editorial revisions are rigorous.

Only those who received the direct transmission of the Buddha’s seal (vyākaraṇa) have been admitted to the ink and paper, while all who merely inherited empty echoes have been subject to deletion and pruning. This may be compared to the nine heavens above.
Yet the sun and stars shine with clarity; amidst ten thousand mirrors, the lamp-beads gleam brightly. Those who have rendered meritorious service at the ancestral temple are by no means few.

Should some criticize this as being too much activity, they would likewise fail to understand that it is here that the future is opened up based on the past, and that the lineage of wisdom depends upon it.
To exclude the heterodox and manifest the orthodox is truly a matter of vital concern for the transmission of the Way; one cannot remain silent about it. For indeed...
When the mirror of Xuanyuan was suspended, Chiyou lost his majesty; with the charts of Baitai, the illusory foxes were extinguished in their tracks.

Thus, those who practice deception and plunder the void are filled with shame, and those who know the Dharma are struck with awe. Is this not sufficient to comfort the original aspiration of the Hundred Chan Masters?

Upon meeting Master Zhou Xu—who is like a divine steed among fragrant elephants and a towering ridgepole for the forest of the Dharma—he read through them once and struck his hand in rhythmic approval, praising them as excellent.
Consequently, the state provided gold for the vanguard procession, and there was not one among the donors of that time who did not respond with inspired zeal upon hearing the news.

Meanwhile, those who had feigned auspicious signs and usurped mandates were completely cleansed away. From this day forward, wherever one goes, one shall be imbued with the fragrance of sandalwood.
To have this drum of lethal poison placed here is truly a distinct lineage of the secret transmission; it is a rare and magnificent occasion.

From this, one certainly knows that once this carving is completed, it shall be a treasure for both the realms of the unseen and the seen. Before long, it will be returned to the Dragon Treasury of Sāgara; will it not then endure together with the vast eons?

A Strict Lineage To begin with, the original intent was revealed by holding up a flower; the smile was a response that struck the core. When the *kṣa* pole was overturned, the golden robe was received.

From this point, the Way of the Separate Transmission Outside the Teachings first arose. This extended from the seven patriarchs of the Western Heaven to the two or three patriarchs of the Eastern Land, none of whom failed to...
By using mustard seeds as rollers and needles, and employing the mechanism to enter the target, the lineage of the Way has thus become long and enduring.
This is truly because of the transmission from above and the initiation from below; the source from which it originates clearly manifests the harmonious affinity between teacher and disciple.

Throughout the many successive generations, there have been no lack of individuals who not only joined their fragrances to aid one another’s beauty, but also ensured its prosperity and flourishing beyond measure.
The sun, moon, and lamps alternate in splendor without any interval between them;
their radiance is so brilliant that from the time of the ancient masters with the "eye," they have emerged like thousands of mountains and ten thousand peaks, shoulder to shoulder.

Each established its own name and doctrine, and for a time, these were mutually illuminated to form distinct schools of thought, eventually resulting in the Five Houses standing side by side throughout successive generations.

In this world, however, whether it be sons or grandsons, if they all grasp [the teaching] face-to-face and realize it directly before them, it will then be transmitted and spread in succession as a long-flowing stream, such that none shall ever obscure its dharma lineage.

What is called the "orthodox tradition" and "correct pulse" that circulates throughout the world is indeed correct in name and consistent in expression; even for ten thousand billion generations, it is sufficient to verify its source and flow.

This is the basis [of our inquiry]. Alas, as the ages have long passed and Heaven has endured for a great length of time, the waxing and waning of destiny and the concealment or manifestation of the Way have caused people to gradually grow dim-sighted;
thus errors have been transmitted one after another, with "fish" and "ru" (homophones) no longer distinguished.

This has led to the situation where several individuals under Longtan Xuanzheng and Deshan Xuanjian all claimed to descend from the lineage of Qingyuan Xingsi and Shitou Xiqian, without realizing that Longtan Xuanzheng...

The descendants of Deshan Xuanjian are numerous and particularly prolific; they truly stem from Mazu Daoyi’s realization of the Heavenly King Samantabhadra, being a direct and authentic transmission, as demonstrated in detail and with utmost clarity in the seventh fascicle of the *Wudeng Huiyuan*.
The two works, the *Rentian Yimou* and the *Fozu Tongzai*, also record this accordingly. Recently, upon reading the *Zongmen Zhengming Lu*, it is even more so.
It is like being confronted with a clear mirror; among those who possess the clear eye within the Dharma-gates, there are none who do not recognize these errors and discrepancies.

Yet, our predecessors remained indifferent and did not take the trouble to correct them by revising the woodblocks, so that it has ultimately become a single volume of doubtful scripture for all eternity, with no end in sight.
From this point on, errors and fabrications have flowed downward. Since both person and dharma must certainly be examined and rectified, this is indeed the case here.

This has also been a matter of concern for the ancient Chan lineage. However, following this period of widespread errors and misconceptions, there was again the case of Jianfu Gu, who, triggered by the words of a former master found upon paper, claimed to be the distant successor of the ancient Yunmen Wenyan.
He did not stop at more than a hundred years [of difference], yet he regarded him as his Dharma-heir teacher, saying: "I refuse to seek another teacher."

The seal [of transmission] was treated by him as something of personal great importance, yet as something of little consequence for the Dharma. Day after day, month after month, his corruptions accumulated ever more deeply, persisting until this day.
Furthermore, he gave rise to non-human beings who failed to understand the pulse of immediate realization and awakening;

they merely pursued their own private interests and illicitly received the entrustment of the lineage, remaining utterly devoid of any dread regarding their lack of understanding of the Dharma. This is truly an offense against the Dharma-gate.

It is difficult to enumerate them all; is this not truly lamentable? There are still those who, having no connection whatsoever, falsely claim to belong to a certain school or to be the descendants of a certain person, and even presume to trace their lineage back to distant ancestors, styling themselves kings or hegemonarchs.

All such individuals have long borrowed these titles without returning them, thereby falling into the same old pitfalls of the past as those of Jianfu Monastery. At first, only one or two engaged in this, yet there are still...

People have frequently experienced alarm and delusion; now it has spread everywhere like a flood. The chaotic order cannot be traced, as pervasive as rice, hemp, bamboo, and reeds, causing confusion and turmoil wherever one goes until it fills the entire world.
Yet no one perceives this, remaining complacent and treating it as nothing strange.

Unexpectedly, the single matter of the Chan school is as heavy as a single thread holding up a cauldron, having persisted until the present day in such a state of turbid evil that it can hardly be grasped.
Its origins are profound and vast—alas, how lamentable! Where shall the Way of the Direct Pointing, transmitted outside the teachings, find its resting place?
Since I first attained a deep resonance with the late Master Mìyún, I have presided over this matter for more than twenty springs.
Observing the errors and fabrications of the past and seeing the confusion prevailing in this world, I have often placed my hand upon my heart in pain, unable to remain at ease.

Thus, for the first time, I became aware of the matters within the School of the Patriarchs (Zongmen). I immediately made a vow to set brush to paper, yet many years have passed without my long-cherished ambition being fulfilled.
Fortunately, in the autumn of the Xinmao year, I was graced by various gentlemen and scholars, each possessing the single eye of discernment, who together compared and corrected [the text].
Consequently, I have now assigned the lineage of Emperor Tiantai’s awakening—along with its sons and grandsons—to the Stone of Qingyuan Si.

Regarding the *Touqian-pu* (Spectacle of the Head’s Relocation): the lineages descending from Longtan Chongxian and Deshan Xuanjian were such that their sons and grandsons still returned to Mazu Daoyi’s Tianwang Huairang branch.
From this point on, as the eye of the school became clear, the genealogical records also became distinct.

Furthermore, the ancient lineage of Jianfu was re-established and listed among those whose dharma heirs were previously unknown. Thus it has continued down to the present day, avoiding the pitfalls of error.

To avoid repeating past errors, I have compiled this work, *The Five Lamps of the Strict Lineage* (*Wǔdēng Yántǒng*). Like other abbreviated records, previous texts were filled with errors and corruptions that circulated freely in the world;

all such works have been scrutinized and rejected. I have selected only the authentic and orthodox lineages of both past and present, specifically those who attained realization through direct encounter and personal transmission, and have compiled them into this volume.
This title reflects the intention that although there are five lamps, they do not depart from the single lamp—each being ignited from it—and it is also intended to strictly uphold the tradition.
I have further collated [the texts] so that the lineage of the Dharma transmitted from antiquity remains free from disorder. Joining the old with the new, there are now twenty-five volumes in total.

Thus, these are the essential scriptures of the Chan school; the life-force of wisdom resides herein, awaiting future worthies and sages who shall come to fully understand the school of direct pointing and single-handed upholding.
That the transmission from master to disciple must proceed in this manner—this is the reality. At this time, [dated].

General Principles for the Five Lamps: A Strict Lineage.

From the time of the Buddhas and patriarchs above, there has been nothing transmitted that was not received through direct oral instruction and personal succession; thus, there must always be a source and a stream to serve as proof of authenticity.

Subsequently, the five schools flourished and their thousand branches vied in splendor, yet the specific points of teacher-to-disciple transmission remained clearly documented and manifest through successive generations. Indeed...

This is what is called "the unifying thread" (*tǒng*). As the unifying thread belongs to the lineage of the Way (*dàomài*) and governs the critical junctures, it cannot tolerate even the slightest bit of fabrication or borrowing.

Were it not for rigorous textual collation and verification, the tracks of foxes would spread everywhere. Therefore, the continuation of the *Bǎozì Tuánjī* and the transmission of the *Dēnglù* are by no means trivial matters;
they must ensure that they were trusted in their own time and provide sufficient evidence for future generations. What is precious lies in being sincere and cautious; thus, the name shall be correct.
The phrasing is strict; it is hoped that this will suffice to strip away the spirit of those who merely inherit echoes and receive reverberations.

Regarding the two lineages descending from Caoxi, the *Zongmen Tongyao Huiyuan* first lists Nanyue and secondly records Qingyuan; these are recorded in the *Huiyuan* and are as brilliant as the sun and stars.
Recently, I have seen the *Xu lüe* (Continued Abridgment), which, in its attempt to continue the *Huiyuan*, instead places Qingyuan first and ranks Nanyue second.
How could Nanyue have privately exalted the ancestor from whom he descended while inverting the order of the lineage book that he himself continued?
Furthermore, both the prophecies concerning the "Horse Colt" (Machu) in India and China designate Nanyue as the primary successor, while Qingyuan is not mentioned therein.
Even by this alone, the sequence of their chronological priority can be determined.

The separate transmission (biezhuan) has one essential point: it does not fall into the realm of words and letters. It is solely the realization and verification attained by those who have personally received the prediction of enlightenment (vyākaraṇa);

only such individuals may record it in the Lamp of the Dharma. If the time since the Sage has grown distant, those who seek to trigger awakening through mere words and phrases must absolutely not attempt to continue the lineage through their own private minds.
Xuancè said: "From the time after Bhīṣmagarjitasvarakalpa onwards, all instances of self-awakening without a teacher belong to the category of 'Heavenly' [attainment]."
Nevertheless, even though the non-Buddhists [had already reached their goal], Yongjia nonetheless sought instruction at Caoxi;
and although Juefan had already attained awakening, he certainly received certification from Zhenjing. This is truly because the succession of masters cannot be dispensed with.
For example, Gu of Jianfu lived more than a hundred years after Yunmen, yet he falsely claimed to be his dharma heir; Jiyin rebuked him for this. Recently, Xueqiao...
Xin followed their narrow tracks and likewise succeeded Yunmen; thus, he took personal bias as his own lineage.
How then can the world and future generations have any standard to rely upon? Once this trend is initiated, where will it end?
Fearing this, I could not refrain from rising to restrain it; therefore, I have listed these two houses side by side under the section "Successors Not Yet Verified."
The *Chuan deng lu* records that Emperor Tianhuang Daowu succeeded Shitou, yet erroneously states that Longtan Chongxin succeeded him;
this led to the claim that the two schools of Yunmen and Fayen originated from Qingyuan. At the time, the investigation was not thorough, and thus for a thousand years it remained a case of doubt.
Now, examining the stele composed by Qiu Xuansu, it is stated that Tianwang Daowu succeeded Mazu.
The Buddha [was his master], and Longtan was his son. Furthermore, examining the stele composed by Fu Zai, it states that Tianhuang Daowu succeeded Shitou and Huizhen received his lineage.
Moreover, the renowned Tang figure Guī Dēng authored the "Stele of Nanyue Huirang," and Quán Deyú wrote the "Epitaph for Mazu";
both record the name of Tianwang Daowu. Thus, the Buddhist community [acknowledges this].
The *Continued Lamp Record* (Xu deng lu) also records that Xuedou Xian was the ninth-generation descendant of Mazu;

the *Comprehensive Record of Buddhas and Patriarchs* (Fozu tongzai) records the same. Therefore, Dachuang, in composing the *Five Lamps Compendium* (Wudeng huiyuan), established this conclusion by cross-referencing two inscriptions:

this is where the essential tenet resides. Although these traditions have been transmitted for a long time, they do not become confused or intermingled.
Rather than citing other examples, let us take Xuefeng as an illustration. While Xuefeng was serving as the head cook at Dongshan, he happened to be washing rice one day.
Mount Yunmen asked, "To sift the sand is to remove the rice; to sift the rice is to remove the sand. Fengxue said, "Sand and rice are removed together.

[The lineage] shifts. Furthermore, from under the guidance of Emperor-Tianhuang Daowu emerged Zhou Jingang, who scolded the winds and reviled the rains;

Why is it that at the point where the hand is extended downward, life and death are not the same? Now, let us verify this with the records of Qiu and Fu;

These words of boundless significance may indeed be called "obtaining the truth through a drop of blood."
Appendix: Venerable Jiyin’s Refutation of Gu Yao’s Succession to Yunmen. The *Línjiàn Lù* states:
"It has been no less than a hundred years since the era of Master Yúnmén, yet Gūtǎzhǔ claims to be his successor."
Qing Huayan had never known the Great Sun; he succeeded him without hesitation solely because of the words of Master Yuan of Fushan.
Both elders transmitted their teachings and conduct as they were, regarding themselves with great gravity yet regarding the Dharma with great lightness.
Among those of antiquity who held the Dharma in high esteem, Huangbo of Yongjia was one such.
Having attained awakening to the essence of the Buddha-mind while reading the *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he went to visit the Sixth Patriarch, saying, "I wish to establish the definitive school.
Huangbo had awakened to the intent of Mazu and succeeded Baizhang; thus, Baizhang sighed that he could not surpass him.

The *Sengbao zhuan* states: "In antiquity, there were three errors in explaining the Dharma: first, judging the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials as having been established by Xuansha’s 'Three Statements';

second, condemning the words of Baling for failing to recognize the 'live phrase'; and third, dividing the 'self' into two types, thereby failing to understand the difficulty with which the sages formulated their teachings.
Regarding the topic of "Literary Chan," the Ancient Pagoda Master (Guta Zhu) discussed the Mysteries and Essentials.
He said, "I have no way to prove his error. It would be satisfying to shake Linji up and make him roar in pain.
He further inscribed a discussion on the two kinds of "self," saying: "The Ancient was indeed a sinner within our Dharma, yet he considered himself able to succeed Yunmen.
The manner in which he deceived himself and others is revealed of its own accord without needing exhaustive investigation. These three words are sufficient.

The Master Jianmu, upon attaining enlightenment, established his own discourse, deeming it unavoidable to establish a lineage through his own composition, yet considering it improper to recklessly claim the patriarchs as his ancestors.

Thus, although the ancient Patriarch Tatu included his name in the *Chuan deng lu*, those who subsequently compiled the records lacked the outstanding insight of Jiyin and were unable to wield the pen of Donggu as courageously;
consequently, they allowed him to be included indiscriminately for the sake of future generations.

This is merely the justification for my audacious presumption. Although I have inscribed my name among those in the *Chuandeng lu* (Records of the Transmission of the Lamp), I ultimately cannot escape various criticisms and rebukes.
The disciplinary framework of the Dharma-gate is as rigorous as this; later generations should take this as a warning. How could they possibly follow such an example?
